  • Explain the Huygens–Fresnel principle and describe how it accounts for the propagation of light
  • waves.
  • The Huygens–Fresnel Principle is one of the most fundamental concepts in wave optics. It provides a
  • complete physical explanation for the propagation of light waves and the phenomenon of diffraction
  • which is the bending of light around obstacles and apertures.(Hecht, §10.1)
  • Original Huygens’s Principle
  • Christian Huygens proposed that every point on a wavefront at a given instant acts as a source of
  • secondary spherical wavelets. The new wavefront at any later instant is simply the envelope of all
  • these secondary wavelets. While this construction successfully predicted the general direction of wave
  • propagation, it had a serious limitation. It made no reference to wavelength and ignored the mutual
  • interaction of the secondary wavelets. As a result, it could not explain why light forms sharp geometric
  • shadows while sound bends easily around large obstacles. The principle was geometrically useful but
  • physically incomplete.
  • Fresnel’s Contribution
  • Fresnel overcame this limitation by introducing the concept of interference into Huygens’s construction.
  • He proposed that the secondary wavelets emitted from each point on the wavefront do not merely
  • form an envelope but superpose with one another. The resultant optical field at any point in space is
  • determined by the combined effect of all these wavelets, taking into account both their amplitudes and
  • their relative phases. This single addition of interference transformed the principle from a geometrical
  • approximation into a powerful physical theory capable of predicting the detailed structure of diffraction
  • patterns.
  • Huygens–Fresnel Principle The Huygens–Fresnel Principle states that every unobstructed point
  • on a wavefront, at a given instant, serves as a source of secondary spherical wavelets having the same
  • frequency as the primary wave. The amplitude of the optical field at any point beyond is the superpo
  • sition of all these wavelets, considering their amplitudes and relative phases.
  • How it Accounts for Propagation of Light Waves
  • The principle explains light propagation through the mechanism of interference among secondary
  • wavelets as follows
  • In the forward direction, the secondary wavelets from all points on the wavefront travel nearly equal
  • path lengths and arrive approximately in phase. They therefore interfere constructively, producing a
  • strong resultant field and sustaining the forward propagation of the wave.
  • In oblique directions, the path lengths from different points on the wavefront to the observation point
  • differ significantly. The wavelets arrive with varying phases and interfere destructively, suppressing the
  • optical field in those directions.

  • Explain the Huygens–Fresnel principle and describe how it accounts for the propagation of light
  • waves.
  • The Huygens–Fresnel Principle is one of the most fundamental concepts in wave optics. It provides a
  • complete physical explanation for the propagation of light waves and the phenomenon of diffraction
  • which is the bending of light around obstacles and apertures.(Hecht, §10.1)
  • Original Huygens’s Principle
  • Christian Huygens proposed that every point on a wavefront at a given instant acts as a source of
  • secondary spherical wavelets. The new wavefront at any later instant is simply the envelope of all
  • these secondary wavelets. While this construction successfully predicted the general direction of wave
  • propagation, it had a serious limitation. It made no reference to wavelength and ignored the mutual
  • interaction of the secondary wavelets. As a result, it could not explain why light forms sharp geometric
  • shadows while sound bends easily around large obstacles. The principle was geometrically useful but
  • physically incomplete.
  • Fresnel’s Contribution
  • Fresnel overcame this limitation by introducing the concept of interference into Huygens’s construction.
  • He proposed that the secondary wavelets emitted from each point on the wavefront do not merely
  • form an envelope but superpose with one another. The resultant optical field at any point in space is
  • determined by the combined effect of all these wavelets, taking into account both their amplitudes and
  • their relative phases. This single addition of interference transformed the principle from a geometrical
  • approximation into a powerful physical theory capable of predicting the detailed structure of diffraction
  • patterns.
  • Huygens–Fresnel Principle The Huygens–Fresnel Principle states that every unobstructed point
  • on a wavefront, at a given instant, serves as a source of secondary spherical wavelets having the same
  • frequency as the primary wave. The amplitude of the optical field at any point beyond is the superpo
  • sition of all these wavelets, considering their amplitudes and relative phases.
  • How it Accounts for Propagation of Light Waves
  • The principle explains light propagation through the mechanism of interference among secondary
  • wavelets as follows
  • In the forward direction, the secondary wavelets from all points on the wavefront travel nearly equal
  • path lengths and arrive approximately in phase. They therefore interfere constructively, producing a
  • strong resultant field and sustaining the forward propagation of the wave.
  • In oblique directions, the path lengths from different points on the wavefront to the observation point
  • differ significantly. The wavelets arrive with varying phases and interfere destructively, suppressing the
  • optical field in those directions.
